Methodology

The audit was performed by the QSI engine 1.3.0. Each analyzer emits facts (rule, parameters, evidence); finding texts are generated from the rule catalog. Methodology sources are listed under "Sources and normative documents".

Prioritization uses an explainable weighted model (severity, exploitability, exposure, confidentiality/integrity/availability impact weighted by the "Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet" profile, asset criticality, urgency, ease of remediation) with a confidence multiplier. CVSS v3.1 is applied only to technical vulnerabilities with a defined vector. Long-term quantum risks use Mosca's inequality; their severity is capped at Medium and they are never presented as exploitable vulnerabilities.

Finding classes: confirmed technical vulnerability; known vulnerable component (a dependency version named in an advisory; whether the affected code is reachable is assessed separately, and a component confirmed by review becomes a vulnerability); confirmed configuration error; potential cryptographic risk; long-term post-quantum risk; improvement recommendation; insufficient data. Heuristic findings are marked preliminary; analyst decisions are shown next to the findings.

Architecture overview

Static review of the source tree canton at 4eab7a047040bb61798b66abde794c8cb27f7746. 3314 files analysed; of 8786 files, 4254 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 1218 are not read by any analyzer, 0 exceed the per-file limit and 0 did not fit the total limit. Files no analyzer reads include: .ci/Dockerfile.canton-build, .ci/Dockerfile.query-stats-postgres, .ci/README.md, .ci/nix-exec, .ci/setup-docker-build-container.sh. 36 files in build-output or dependency-cache directories (.git, .hg, .venv, __pycache__, build, dist, node_modules, target, vendor, venv) were not read. No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

QSI-2026-19406 · KEY-PRIVATE-IN-INPUTHigh

Private key material present in performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem

Confirmed technical vulnerabilityConfidence: High

A 'PRIVATE KEY' block was found at line 1 of performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem. QSI redacted the key before storage; the original file still contains it.

Affected asset
file:performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem
Data source
performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem
Detection method
PEM header detection.
Analyzer
certificates 1.3.0 · 2026-11-06 15:24 UTC
Priority score
76.8 / 100 (Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet)
CVSS v3.1
8.1 — CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N

Potential impact

Anyone with access to this file (repository, backups, CI logs) can impersonate the key owner or decrypt protected data.

Reproduction steps

grep -n 'PRIVATE KEY-----' performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem

Evidence

file_excerpt · performance/src/main/console/tls/participant.pem · line 1 · SHA-256 8ff5675e3f073e63… · File 41b6c1b1fe89bcc3…
Line 1: -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- … [REDACTED BY QSI] … -----END …

Limitations of the check

QSI cannot determine whether this key is in production use. The key value was not retained.

Recommendation

Treat the key as compromised: rotate it, revoke associated certificates, remove it from version history and store keys in a secrets manager/HSM.

Retest procedure

Search the repository and its history for private key headers; confirm the old key is revoked.

Limitations of the check

This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.

Recommendation

Wrap keys with ML-KEM or a hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) and re-wrap the stored keys; data that may already have been copied needs its own assessment.

Retest procedure

Re-run the inventory after refactoring.

Long-term post-quantum riskConfidence: High

The certificate localhost uses a RSA 4096-bit public key, valid until 2024-01-11. RSA is broken by Shor's algorithm on a CRQC.

Affected asset
certificate:localhost
Data source
performance/src/main/console/tls/synchronizer.crt
Detection method

Analyzer
certificates 1.3.0 · 2026-11-06 15:24 UTC
Priority score

CVSS v3.1
not applicable
Mosca's inequality (x + y > z)
x=0.0, y=5.0, z=8.0 → time available under this scenario

Potential impact

For authentication, risk materializes only once a CRQC exists while the key/certificate is still trusted. Certificates are short-lived, so the main concern is the PKI and long-lived roots/intermediates.

Reproduction steps

openssl x509 -in performance/src/main/console/tls/synchronizer.crt -noout -text | grep -A2 'Public Key Algorithm'

Limitations of the check

This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability.

Recommendation

Track in the PQC inventory; prefer short certificate lifetimes; follow CA/Browser Forum and NIST PQC transition guidance for ML-DSA certificates.

Retest procedure

Re-audit once PQC or hybrid certificates are deployed.

Post-quantum maturity: Level 2 of 4 — post-quantum in use outside the critical paths

  • In use: ML-DSA — community/app-base/src/main/scala/com/digitalasset/canton/admin/api/client/data/crypto/Signing.scala
  • In use: ML-DSA — community/base/src/main/scala/com/digitalasset/canton/crypto/Signing.scala
  • Classical only — key wrapping and data encryption at rest: ECDH (10 file(s))

Next step: Extend post-quantum protection to the critical roles that stay classical, starting with what can be recorded today (wrapped keys, channel key exchange).

Levels: 0 none; 1 present, not wired; 2 in use outside the critical paths; 3 hybrid in a critical path; 4 post-quantum by default in the critical paths (root of trust, key wrapping, channel key exchange). Judged from code and manifests.

What the quantum-vulnerable algorithms do

RoleAlgorithms (files)IDFirst step
key wrapping and data encryption at restECDH (10)QSI-2026-19399Wrap keys with ML-KEM or a hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) and re-wrap the stored keys; data that may already have been copied needs its own assessment
transaction and message signingECDSA (1), Ed25519 (1), RSA (1)QSI-2026-19395, QSI-2026-19396, QSI-2026-19397Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them
authentication and identity (certificates, tokens, device attestation)RSA (2), ECDSA (1), Ed25519 (1)QSI-2026-19398, QSI-2026-19401, QSI-2026-19402Keep credentials short-lived and plan ML-DSA certificates, tokens and keys as the ecosystem supports them
role not determinedECDSA (9), RSA (2)QSI-2026-19394, QSI-2026-19400Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility

Roles are judged from file paths, function names and the code around each match; review confirms them. Root-of-trust keys and wrapped keys come first: they are hard to replace or can be recorded today.

z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

Quantum algorithms relevant to this inventory

Quantum algorithmEffectInventoried algorithms (rows)What it means for this audit
Shor's algorithm — factoring
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		breaks RSA (8)Breaks RSA at every key length: a longer modulus only raises the cost polynomially. Plan migration to ML-KEM (or a hybrid) for key establishment and ML-DSA / SLH-DSA for signatures; start with keys protecting data that must stay confidential for years (harvest now, decrypt later) and with long-lived signatures.
Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		breaks ECDH (10), ECDSA (17), Ed25519 (2)Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) AES-128 (8), BLAKE2 (1), BLAKE3 (1), HMAC (20), IDEA (1), Keccak-256 (1), SHA-2 (7)Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) BLAKE2 (1), BLAKE3 (1), Keccak-256 (1), SHA-2 (7)256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
Quantum lattice sieving
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		included in standard parameters ML-DSA (2)No change for ML-KEM or ML-DSA at the standard parameter sets. A 2024 claim of a polynomial-time quantum LWE algorithm was withdrawn after a bug was found (see claims).

Effects: breaks — replace the algorithm; weakens — larger keys or outputs restore the margin; included in standard parameters — no action at standard parameter sets; only with superposition queries — not applicable to ordinary deployments.

  • z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

low

QSI-2026-19399 · P4 · 90 daysroot-cause fix

Plan migration of ECDH to Hybrid key establishment with ML-KEM (FIPS 203), e.g. X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 or mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH (or a hybrid scheme) once supported by your libraries, protocols and counterparties.

Rationale
Removes dependence on a quantum-vulnerable public-key primitive.
Expected outcome
The asset uses a NIST-standardized post-quantum or hybrid algorithm.
Complexity
high
Dependencies
Library/protocol support (e.g. OpenSSL ≥ 3.5, HSM firmware), interoperability with peers.
Side effects
Larger keys/signatures, possible performance and compatibility impact.
Tests before change
Interoperability tests in a staging environment.
Tests after change
Verify the negotiated/used algorithm on the production asset.
Closure criteria
Re-audit shows Hybrid key establishment with ML-KEM (FIPS 203), e.g. X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 or mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH or a hybrid scheme in use.

  2. A. Chailloux, J. Loyer — Lattice sieving via quantum random walks (ASIACRYPT 2021; IACR ePrint 2021/570) — IACR ePrint. https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/570 (peer-reviewed article: 2^{0.2570d + o(d)}, previously 2^{0.2653d + o(d)} (Laarhoven))

Schrottenloher — An Efficient Quantum Collision Search Algorithm and Implications on Symmetric Cryptography (ASIACRYPT 2017; IACR ePrint 2017/847) — IACR ePrint. https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/847 (peer-reviewed article: Õ(2^{2n/5}) time, O(n) qubits, Õ(2^{n/5}) classical memory)

  5. C. Gidney — How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits (arXiv:2505.15917) — arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917 (preprint (2025-05-21): < 1 million noisy qubits, < 1 week, 0.1% gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle)
  6. C. Gidney, M. Ekerå — How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits (Quantum 5, 433) — Quantum. https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2021-04-15-433 (peer-reviewed article (2021): 10^-3 gate error, 1 µs cycle, 10 µs reaction time)
  7. C. Zalka — Grover's quantum searching algorithm is optimal (Phys. Rev. A 60, 2746, 1999; arXiv:quant-ph/9711070) — APS. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.60.2746 (peer-reviewed article: optimal for any success probability; parallel search gains no more than splitting the space)

  11. D. Litinski — How to compute a 256-bit elliptic curve private key with only 50 million Toffoli gates (arXiv:2306.08585) — arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08585 (preprint (2023-06-14): 6000 modules × 1152 physical qubits, one key per 10 minutes under its architecture assumptions)

Amy et al. — Estimating the cost of generic quantum pre-image attacks on SHA-2 and SHA-3 (SAC 2016; arXiv:1603.09383) — Springer / arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09383 (peer-reviewed article: SHA-256 about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits; SHA3-256 about 2^146.5 cycles on 2^20)
  19. M. Cain et al. — Shor's algorithm is possible with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits (arXiv:2603.28627) — arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28627 (preprint (2026-03-30): P-256 in a few days with 26,000 physical neutral-atom qubits; RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude longer)

A composite (hybrid) key establishment stays FIPS 140-validatable while one input comes from an approved scheme. Repeats the federal deadlines of OMB M-26-15: post-quantum key establishment by 2030-12-31 and signatures by 2031-12-31 for high value assets and high impact systems)
